utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone in the courtroom. Mr. Registrar, could you call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case number IT-04-75-T, the Prosecutor versus Goran Hadzic. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Could we have appearances, please, starting with the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honour, Sarah Clanton and Matthew Olmsted for the Prosecution, with our intern Maria Bukovac.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Zivanovic, for the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. For the Defence of Goran Hadzic, Zoran Zivanovic and Christopher Gosnell. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you. The witness may be brought in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Witness. Do you hear me in a language you understand.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good morning. [Interpretation] Yes, I can hear you well in the Croatian language.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you for coming to The Hague to assist the Tribunal. Could you please state your full name and date of birth, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My name is Stipan Kraljevic, 8th of January, 19 --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please repeat the year.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction, 1937.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kraljevic, you are about to make the solemn declaration by which witnesses commit themselves to tell the truth. I have to point out to you that by doing so you expose yourself to the penalties of perjury should you give false or untruthful information to the Tribunal. Can I ask you now to read the solemn declaration the court usher will give to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. You may be seated.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You're welcome.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Ms. Clanton, your witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Kraljevic.

utterances.speaker: STIPAN KRALJEVIC
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: With the permission of the Court, I'd like to lead the witness through his background information.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Please do.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: Mr. Kraljevic, is it correct that you were born in Bosnia and moved to Croatia in the early 1940s?

utterances.speaker: STIPAN KRALJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: And is it correct that you completed your gymnasium studies in Backa Palanka?

utterances.speaker: STIPAN KRALJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: And that you did your compulsory service with the JNA in Montenegro from 1961 to 1962?

utterances.speaker: STIPAN KRALJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: Mr. Kraljevic, is it correct that you then studied agriculture at the university in Zagreb?

utterances.speaker: STIPAN KRALJEVIC
utterances.text: I studied and graduated before I went to do my compulsory military service.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: Thank you for that. The place where you studied, was that in Zagreb?

utterances.speaker: STIPAN KRALJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: And is it correct that you obtained further certification to be a teacher?

utterances.speaker: STIPAN KRALJEVIC
utterances.text: Since I worked in school, a number of teaching subjects had to be passed and that is what I did. I did those exams.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: And is it correct that in 1990 you were working as a lecturer in the topic of agriculture?

utterances.speaker: STIPAN KRALJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: Mr. Kraljevic, can you confirm that you served as mayor of Ilok starting in 1993?

utterances.speaker: STIPAN KRALJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, between 1993 and 2001.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: And is it correct that the -- in 1990, the town of Ilok was part of the municipality of Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: STIPAN KRALJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: And is it correct that the towns of Sarengrad, Bapska, and Mohovo are part of the local community of Ilok?

utterances.speaker: STIPAN KRALJEVIC
utterances.text: As a matter of fact, those were all local communes of the municipality of Vukovar. That was one single municipality, yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: And, Mr. Kraljevic, how far is Ilok from Vukovar, the city of Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: STIPAN KRALJEVIC
utterances.text: 35 kilometres.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: And can you tell us, please, the population in Ilok in March of 1991 in terms of the number of people who were living there?

utterances.speaker: STIPAN KRALJEVIC
utterances.text: In Ilok itself, there were 6.774 inhabitants according to the 1991 census. Now, in the villages surrounding Ilok, Bapska, there was about 1600; Sarengrad, 1100; and Orahovo, 340.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: Mr. Kraljevic, what was the majority ethnic group in Ilok?

utterances.speaker: STIPAN KRALJEVIC
utterances.text: In ethnical term, Ilok was a mixed settlement. However, the population of the Ilok, the majority of it, were Croats, who accounted for about 64 per cent. There were 7 per cent Serbs, 17 per cent of Slovaks, which was the largest ethnic minority in the town of Ilok and we can easily say in all of the Croatia as well. As for other ethnic minorities, their numbers were really small.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: Mr. Kraljevic, the villages that you've described as being part of the Ilok area, Sarengrad, Bapska, Mohovo, what was the majority ethnicity in those villages?

utterances.speaker: STIPAN KRALJEVIC
utterances.text: Over 30 [as interpreted] per cent in Sarengrad and Bapska were Croats, 4 per cent were Serbs, 64 per cent Croats in Mohovo and 3 per cent Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: And, Mr. Kraljevic, just to follow up on that, can you tell us again what was the percentage of Croats in Sarengrad, please?

utterances.speaker: STIPAN KRALJEVIC
utterances.text: Over 90 per cent.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: And in Bapska?

utterances.speaker: STIPAN KRALJEVIC
utterances.text: Over 90 per cent.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, earlier you confirmed that you completed your studies at the gymnasium level in Backa Palanka. I'd like to ask you if it was common for residents of Ilok and Backa Palanka to have business and studies on both sides of the Danube River?

utterances.speaker: STIPAN KRALJEVIC
utterances.text: I attended to the secondary school in Backa Palanka between '56 and '61. At the time there was an agricultural school in Ilok. There was a secondary grammar school in Backa Palanka. Children normally attended both schools according to their preferences. The people from Ilok attended the grammar school and the others came to Backa Palanka to attend the agricultural school.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: And how are these two towns connected geographically?

utterances.speaker: STIPAN KRALJEVIC
utterances.text: Both towns are located on both banks of the Danube River and they were connected by a ferry. Then in 1974, a bridge between Backa Palanka and Ilok was built. This bridge was very important especially for Vojvodina because that was the shortest way with the western part.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: What was the name of this bridge?

utterances.speaker: STIPAN KRALJEVIC
utterances.text: Its name was the 21st of May in order to mark the birthday of President Tito.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: And, Mr. Kraljevic, you've told us about the fact that you attended school in Backa Palanka yourself and that it was common for people to cross to go about their daily functions. I want to ask you, can you describe the relations in 1990 with your neighbours in Serbia?

utterances.speaker: STIPAN KRALJEVIC
utterances.text: The movement of people went normally. I did not observe any problems in that respect.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: Were you a member of any political party in 1990 or shortly thereafter?

utterances.speaker: STIPAN KRALJEVIC
utterances.text: Up until 1990, 1991, I hadn't been a member of any party. I was only a member of the Croatian Christian Democratic Party. However, this party did not survive for too long and it was disbanded in 1993.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Kraljevic. I would now like to change topics and ask you about what you observed happening in 1991, specifically changes in your community in 1991. I want to ask you if there came a time that you noticed any changes in behaviour between the ethnic groups in your area?

utterances.speaker: STIPAN KRALJEVIC
utterances.text: Well, it did not actually start only in 1990, it had been lasting for quite some time because this atmosphere was felt in the central committees of certain republics who were in disagreement. This was followed by self-rule elections both on the republican and local levels.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: And, Mr. Kraljevic, our time is limited so I'd like to focus you on what you observed in 1991, please. Did you see any changes in your area in 1991?

utterances.speaker: STIPAN KRALJEVIC
utterances.text: The local government was changed following the elections, which means there were many new members. In 1991, during the preparations for multi-party elections, an incident took place in Ilok at the Orthodox cemetery where a number of graves were desecrated or demolished, and I'm talking about the Orthodox cemetery in Ilok.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: Mr. Kraljevic, can you tell us what you learned about how these acts had been committed?

utterances.speaker: STIPAN KRALJEVIC
utterances.text: We didn't hear anything about it because the police, who were 200 metres away, did not respond in any way; however, the journalists from the Novi Sad television were there on the spot on the very same morning and they broadcast this news. That is how this incident was recorded. We can only speculate about who was behind it.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: How did the fact that television from Novi Sad reported on this incident prior to the police, how did that make you understand what had happened there?

utterances.speaker: STIPAN KRALJEVIC
utterances.text: The residents, including myself, perceived this as a provocation and a means of a feeling of sort of mistrust towards certain ethnic groups, but as I said, we might just speculate about who the perpetrators were.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: And, Mr. Kraljevic, were you aware of an event in May 1991 in Borovo Selo?

utterances.speaker: STIPAN KRALJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. We knew because it was on the news, a serious crime was committed in which 12 policemen lost their lives and, of course, this caused high tensions among the populous.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: And what happened in the immediate area of Ilok after this incident at Borovo Selo which you've told us caused high tension among the population?

utterances.speaker: STIPAN KRALJEVIC
utterances.text: Rumours were being spread, all sorts of rumours. Of course there were various stories going around, but the killing of such a large number of police officers naturally caused tensions. But in addition to that, there were rumours being spread that the same thing might be repeated in Ilok as well. As a result, certain individuals, but in working together with the police, started guarding the entry point to Ilok and Bapska from all sides as well as in other settlements. In that way, a duty post was established at the bridge which was manned by members of the civilian protection and that was all.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: Mr. Kraljevic, after the people in Ilok heard about this incident and the civilian protection was put on the bridge, can you describe the response from the other side of the bridge?

utterances.speaker: STIPAN KRALJEVIC
utterances.text: Well, you know, since this duty post was established at the bridge, it provided control of the movement in a way which meant that people passing by were identified, their documents were checked, but this did not hinder any free movement. However, on the 10th of May, on the access to the bridge from Backa, tanks arrived and were positioned at the very entry point to Ilok near the bridge and thereby established their own checkpoint. The explanation was that they wanted to control the traffic in order to prevent any disturbances in that respect.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: Mr. Kraljevic, these tanks you've described, which army did they belong to?

utterances.speaker: STIPAN KRALJEVIC
utterances.text: The Yugoslav People's Army.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: And you've told us that this occurred on the 10th of May; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: STIPAN KRALJEVIC
utterances.text: I believe that it was on the 7th, but I cannot be certain.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: Thank you. And this is in May. After the declaration of independence in June of 1991, what changes did you observe among the Serbs in Ilok?

utterances.speaker: STIPAN KRALJEVIC
utterances.text: Well, I cannot say that there occurred any changes worth mentioning. People were communicating normally. I believe that the relations between neighbours were good; however, there were a few occurrences when certain members of the Serb ethnic group went to Backa Palanka to spend the night there and would then return in the morning under the pretext of doing it for safety reasons, but we didn't notice any need for anyone doing that.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Kraljevic. Can you tell the Court, please, what changes happened within the police after the declaration in June of 1991?

utterances.speaker: STIPAN KRALJEVIC
utterances.text: Well, the composition of the police force compared to the national composition in Croatia was disadvantageous for Croats. About 50 per cent of the population of Croatia in certain parts were Croats and there were parts where Serbs constituted more than 30 per cent and the rest declare themselves of Yugoslavs, although I don't know what that meant. And by that, I mean that there was no Yugoslav nation as such. May I continue?

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Kraljevic, if I could just focus your answer. What I'd like to know is the changes that you could tell us about the police in June of 1991.

utterances.speaker: STIPAN KRALJEVIC
utterances.text: Well, this is precisely what I told you. The number of Croatian policemen increased within the police force. However, after the Republic of Croatia was declared independent, which was followed by the changes to the constitution and multi-party elections, Croatia had new national symbols and these symbols were prescribed as something to be worn on the caps by policemen, and I'm talking about the Croatian coat of arms. However, some policemen refused to wear such caps. As far as I know, they went to Backa Palanka. I think there were five police officers who took that course.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: Thank you. Earlier you've told us that Vukovar is located approximately 35 kilometres from Ilok. I want to ask you if in the summer of 1991 you became aware of an attack in Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: STIPAN KRALJEVIC
utterances.text: I worked at the secondary school centre in Ilok. It catered to the whole municipality of Vukovar, and we had meetings. During the summer, I went to Vukovar for that reason and I also heard news about the situation in Vukovar itself. The situation was complex because barricades had been put up all around, and Vukovar was cut off from Vinkovci. It was cut off at Brsadin and towards Osijek, at Trpinje in the direction of Dalj and Borovo Selo. That would be briefly it. And of course the population couldn't move about freely, which certainly resulted in some tension.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: And from Ilok, what could you hear from this area?

utterances.speaker: STIPAN KRALJEVIC
utterances.text: Radio and television were still operating. People were travelling to Vukovar and back. There was coverage of any event that had happened anywhere.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: And from Ilok, was the fighting audible?

utterances.speaker: STIPAN KRALJEVIC
utterances.text: Well, no, but when, on the 24th of August, an overall attack at Vukovar began, we heard it from Ilok because airplanes flew over Ilok at very low altitude. We could also hear bombing. However, we had heard bombing at Ilok before. If I may, I would like to mention some events that are characteristic of Ilok when some incidents happened.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: Mr. Kraljevic, just to clarify the point that you were just making. Whose aircraft could you hear?

utterances.speaker: STIPAN KRALJEVIC
utterances.text: There was only one organised army and that was the Yugoslav People's Army.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: Thank you. And I do want to ask you now about specific incidents in Ilok between the JNA tanks that you've described for us that were on the bridge and the forces, the civilian protection that was in Ilok. Can you tell us what happened in July of 1991?

utterances.speaker: STIPAN KRALJEVIC
utterances.text: In July 1991, it was on the 8th of July to be precise, an incident happened in the evening hours. As I have already said, by the bridge there was a tank unit of the Yugoslav People's Army. Some 100 metres away, the police of the MUP of Croatia had its own checkpoint. As I've said, the distance between the two was about 100 metres. Suddenly, a tank-mounted machine-gun was used to destroy a vehicle belonging to Ilok police station. There were four persons in that vehicle, one of whom was killed immediately and the others were wounded. They were taken to hospital in Slavonski Brod.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: Mr. Kraljevic, this person who was killed, can you tell the Trial Chamber his age or where he was from?

utterances.speaker: STIPAN KRALJEVIC
utterances.text: The person was from Sarengrad. It was a young man who had only recently joined the police station in Ilok. He may have been 20 or a bit over 20 years old at the time.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: Mr. Kraljevic, what was the response from the police that had been at the checkpoint to being fired on by this machine-gun that was on a tank?

utterances.speaker: STIPAN KRALJEVIC
utterances.text: Nearby, how near exactly I don't know, there was probably a person belonging to the ZNG and that man destroyed a tank with a hand-held rocket launcher, a Zolja.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: And what was the response by the JNA when their tank was destroyed by the hand-held rocket launcher?

utterances.speaker: STIPAN KRALJEVIC
utterances.text: Of course there was a protest by the JNA representative but on the next day around noon, something happened at Principovac. There was a group of ZNG members there who had come to Ilok before that and two aircraft opened machine-gun fire on that group of ZNG members, who were playing soccer at that time. One person was killed and I believe that two were wounded.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: How far is Principovac from Ilok?

utterances.speaker: STIPAN KRALJEVIC
utterances.text: If I may, let me just mention that. In July -- it was in July that this incident happened, but on the other side of our local community in the direction of Sid, a group of JNA members with tanks arrived and took up positions there so that Ilok, from that moment on, was completely surrounded. That would be a short account of these events. However, let me also add that the ZNG, who were accommodated at an agricultural facility, moved to town for safety reasons because JNA contingents were very close. But after that incident I have just mentioned, the ZNG left the area.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: Thank you. If you could tell the Chamber, please, how far Principovac is from Ilok?

utterances.speaker: STIPAN KRALJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. First of all, Ilok is on the promontory next to the Danube at an altitude of about 70 metres. There is another such promontory that we call Principovac which is some 2 kilometres from the centre of Ilok, and there was an excellent view from there. You could see the entire area around Ilok.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: Thank you. As you've just told us, there was a JNA response which was to use aircraft to attack this position in Principovac of -- and the agricultural building of the ZNG. I want to ask, were any other buildings shelled in Ilok at this time?

utterances.speaker: STIPAN KRALJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: Can you tell us which buildings, please?

utterances.speaker: STIPAN KRALJEVIC
utterances.text: It happened on the 20th of July, I think, by the bridge on the Ilok side, of course. There was a private workshop -- that is actually a workshop and a store. It was called Zec. Suddenly, that workshop was attacked with artillery and it was damaged. At the same time, the spire of the Catholic church in Ilok was targeted and damaged, so were some private houses. Fortunately, nobody was killed. As far as I know, only one person was wounded.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: Mr. Kraljevic, I now want to move to talk about events that were happening in the other villages that are near Ilok in the Western Srem region. This would be in the summer and fall of 1991. I'm going to ask you, when did you first hear about the use of aircraft or other JNA equipment in towns or villages in Western Srem?

utterances.speaker: STIPAN KRALJEVIC
utterances.text: I cannot hear the interpretation. Now I can hear it. I cannot hear anything.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: I will ask my question again. I want to ask you, when did you first hear about events in other towns and villages in Western Srem involving the JNA?

utterances.speaker: STIPAN KRALJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Let me try to focus. There are many villages there. Let me -- I'll try to get my bearings. On the border towards Sid, there is Tovarnik, on the road from Sid to Vinkovci. But even before that, there were incidents at Sotin.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: Mr. Kraljevic, perhaps I can focus my question a bit more. Prior to the events in Sotin and Tovarnik, were you aware of any other town or village in the area that had been involved in attack with the JNA. The time period I'm interested in is the late summer of 1991.

utterances.speaker: STIPAN KRALJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. In the late summer of 1991, and if I remember well, it was on the 24th of August when the real attack of the JNA on Vukovar began. On the 25th of August, there were air raids, and at that moment, four persons were killed in a car. Two of them were from Ilok who happened to be in Vukovar. Of course, that was very discomforting. As of the 24th, there was daily combat activity in Vukovar, which was very worrying. Sotin is the first village in the direction of Ilok when you come from Vukovar. It was attacked by aircraft on the 28th of August, I think. It's very telling because at that very time, there was a funeral at Sotin and that added to the dismay over the air raid. From the 5th of September, there was no more communication between Ilok and Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: Mr. Kraljevic, a moment ago you mentioned Tovarnik. I want to ask you what happened in Tovarnik and if you can give us an approximate date?

utterances.speaker: STIPAN KRALJEVIC
utterances.text: There was an ultimatum issued to Tovarnik that they should surrender to the JNA, otherwise the army would enter by force. As far as I know, Mr. Burik, the priest, went to Sid to negotiate but to no avail. And there was an attack on the 24th of September. Many people from Tovarnik came to Ilok through Lovas and some of them went in the other direction, through Nijemci, and Tovarnik was left without the majority of its inhabitants.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: And, Mr. Kraljevic, you've told us that there was this attack on Tovarnik after there was an ultimatum that was received and there were negotiations that didn't lead anywhere. Can you describe for the Chamber what you know about how the attack was actually carried out, what the steps were, and who was engaging in the attack?

utterances.speaker: STIPAN KRALJEVIC
utterances.text: Well, you know, I wasn't there and I can't give you a full description. But infantry and tanks of the army entered the village and so did paramilitaries. I know that there were many victims at Tovarnik but I don't want to speculate about their numbers. I know that some 60 to 80 people were killed there in those few days.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: And what you've described happening in Tovarnik, did this happen in other villages in Western Srem, similar events?

utterances.speaker: STIPAN KRALJEVIC
utterances.text: Of course the main target was Vukovar and the army proceeded -- or, rather, was moving there gradually. I could mention Ilaca, where similar events happened over a course of a few days. And other villages such as Lovas, which is near to Ilok, there was also an ultimatum issued. There was always shelling from heavy weapons. At Tovarnik, for example, many houses were badly damaged. The Catholic church was totally destroyed, and the same thing started at Lovas and in other villages closer to Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: And, Mr. Kraljevic, the villages that you've named, Ilaca, Lovas, can you tell us what was the majority ethnic group in those villages.

utterances.speaker: STIPAN KRALJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I can tell you. Based on the census, over 60 per cent of the population of Tovarnik were Croats and some 30 per cent were Serbs. At Lovas, over 90 per cent of the population was Croatian and there were about 7 per cent Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: Now I would like the assistance of the Registrar, please, to call up 65 ter 06329.1. This is Prosecution Exhibit 1723. And for this to be on the monitor for the witness, please. It's a road map of eastern Croatia and it's at tab 58.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Just for the record, this is Exhibit P1723. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: Mr. Kraljevic, do you see a map on the screen in front of you?

utterances.speaker: STIPAN KRALJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: I would like to ask, please, for the usher's assistance to provide Mr. Kraljevic with a pen that he can use to mark on the map.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Kraljevic, I would like for you to draw a circle around the villages that were attacked in the way that you've previously described.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: And sorry, perhaps we can zoom in a bit. Is it possible? I'm interested in the area south and east of Vukovar, please. A bit to the right. Would it be possible to go a bit further so that we can see to the Croatian border? That's great. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: Mr. Kraljevic, if you could circle the towns that you know experienced events, experienced attacks like the ones you've just described?

utterances.speaker: STIPAN KRALJEVIC
utterances.text: Tovarnik, Ilaca, Lovas, and before that, we mentioned Sotin.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: Were there any other villages that were attacked in the fall of 1991?

utterances.speaker: STIPAN KRALJEVIC
utterances.text: It was further away from us so news didn't travel so easily, but we know that there were incidents at Berak, and in these villages, Cakovci, Tompojevci and Miklusevci. I don't think I need to go further west. I know that in this triangle, Tompojevci, Miklusevci, Cakovci, there is a rather strong ethnic minority of Ukrainians and Ruthenians.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: And, Mr. Kraljevic, you've told us about the villages that were little a bit further away from Ilok, were there any villages going in the direction of Ilok that you recall were also attacked?

utterances.speaker: STIPAN KRALJEVIC
utterances.text: We can mention Bapska and Sarengrad first. It was on the 4th -- just a minute. It was the 4th of October when, around noon, Sarengrad was suddenly attacked with artillery and boats from the Danube and from the other side of the Danube by forces of the JNA. That part of Sarengrad is easily visible from the other bank of the Danube. Sarengrad is on the river itself, and many houses were damaged and so was the Orthodox church, which can be seen very well. There's also a Catholic church there but it was not damaged because it wasn't so easily visible. A civilian was killed and two members of the civil protection were killed in a car. They happened to be there in that car and got killed.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: I'm going to ask you to pause there. I see that you've circled the town of Lovas. Can you tell me how many people were killed in Lovas when it was attacked?

utterances.speaker: STIPAN KRALJEVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, may I first finish with Sarengrad because Bapska was attacked on that very same day, the 4th. Representatives of the JNA were deployed to the south of Sid. Many houses were damaged and a few people were wounded, and with it, I would end. Now, to come to Lovas, this happened practically a week later, if this was on the 4th, and then again on the 10th, Lovas came under attack. As a result, according to the information I received from the observers some time later, 22 casualties were -- and all of them were civilians.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: And, Mr. Kraljevic, you've shown us where these villages are that were attacked. Can you describe for us -- you don't need to mark anything, just tell us in which direction the majority of the people fled after their towns had been attacked?

utterances.speaker: STIPAN KRALJEVIC
utterances.text: Speaking of Lovas and Opatovac, which is on the very bank of the Danube, this is Opatovac, this is Mohovo, the only possibility for the population to withdraw and flee was towards Ilok. There was no other option. Similarly, the population of Sarengrad and/or Bapska were also withdrawing towards Ilok so that at that time, there was a large number of civilians in Ilok, and there were fewer and fewer of facilities providing conditions for normal life, which, of course, caused problems for the residents of Ilok.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: I want to stop you there. Just so that we can be done with this map, you now circled Opatovac and Mohovo. And for the record, I just want to make clear, have you circled these towns because they were attacked and the people fled?

utterances.speaker: STIPAN KRALJEVIC
utterances.text: No, they were not attacked.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: So that we can record the information that you've given to us, I would like for you to please mark next to Opatovac and Mohovo the letter N so we can record that they were not attacked, please.

utterances.speaker: STIPAN KRALJEVIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: Could you -- I'm sorry, I know it's difficult to use the pen. I think that will be a bit difficult to read. Could you please mark again the letter N next to Opatovac and Mohovo for the record.

utterances.speaker: STIPAN KRALJEVIC
utterances.text: [Marks]. I have no experience with this kind of pen, therefore I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: It's okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: At this time the Prosecution would seek to tender this map as marked by the witness, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P1723 marked by the witness in court shall be assigned Exhibit Number P2017. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: And we can take that down, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: Mr. Kraljevic, a moment ago you were describing the events in Bapska, and previously you told us about ultimatums that were delivered to the residents of these towns. I wanted to ask you if you ever had occasion to see a copy of such an ultimatum?

utterances.speaker: STIPAN KRALJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: I would like to ask for the Registrar to please bring up 65 ter 00418, which is P316. This is tab 11.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can see it.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: Mr. Kraljevic, do you recognise this as a document that you provided to the investigators of the OTP?

utterances.speaker: STIPAN KRALJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: Are you able to tell the Trial Chamber the name of the person who authored this?

utterances.speaker: STIPAN KRALJEVIC
utterances.text: The author of this document is last name Barjaktarevic, first name probably Slobodan, but I'm sure about his last name, Major Barjaktarevic. He issued this document and sent it with Boro Tomic, who was working at Mesnica in Sid. He was a resident of Sid, but in the past he used to live in Bapska. And he was the one who handed over the document to representatives of the local commune.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: Mr. Kraljevic, do you recall the names of the representatives of the local commune who received this document?

utterances.speaker: STIPAN KRALJEVIC
utterances.text: Their names were Bozinovic and Rukavina. I believe that those were the Rukavina brothers, Tomislav and -- I don't know exactly the first name of the other one. Rukavina.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: And after this ultimatum was provided to these persons who were the representatives of Bapska, what happened in Bapska?

utterances.speaker: STIPAN KRALJEVIC
utterances.text: Naturally, this document was exceptionally threatening in nature and the population found it very hard to reach a decision. However, the fulfillment of such conditions was not possible and a large number of the inhabitants left for Ilok.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: And earlier you told us that there was an attack on Ilok. How did you first hear about this document -- I'm sorry, an attack on Bapska, excuse me.

utterances.speaker: STIPAN KRALJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I received this document from an office in Zagreb. It was handed over to me by the representative of the Institute for History, while they had received it from the TV station. Presumably it had been given to the journalists by the local residents, and that is how the document found its way to the Institute for History and eventually to Ilok and me.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: What I want to ask you is at the time, so close to the time of the date of this document and then the attack on Bapska, how did you receive information that such a document had been provided? I don't mean actually seeing the document but just that there was such a document that had been provided?

utterances.speaker: STIPAN KRALJEVIC
utterances.text: They received information at the civilian protection HQ. I was not a member of the civilian protection staff and I didn't know anything about it at the time. I learned about this only a few days later, but yes, the civilian protection staff. Because from Bapska, they immediately went to the civilian protection staff to obtain information because, of course, once the attack on Bapska started, members of the civilian protection forces joined the defence of Bapska.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: Mr. Kraljevic, you've told us before that after these towns including Bapska were attacked, the majority of the civilian population fled to Ilok. I would like for you to explain briefly, describe the conditions in Ilok with the refugees coming in.

utterances.speaker: STIPAN KRALJEVIC
utterances.text: There was a huge number of civilians who found shelter in Ilok. The Red Cross of Ilok made arrangements for their accommodation in private houses in socially-owned facilities, various halls, et cetera, so that there was an enormous number of people in the town itself. Even in my own house, there were six people from Lovas whom we put up. They were mostly moving around the centre of town but would come over to spend the night. It was a tense situation. It was difficult. We only had four GPs. There were no medicines and the situation was very difficult. I can tell you that in the course of all those days, life nevertheless went normally, so to say. There was even a bus service for as long as it was possible to maintain it, and I'm talking about the service between Ilok and Backa Palanka. Cazmatrans, the company serviced the route from Ilok, and there was another Serbian company driving from Backa Palanka. However, on one day, while Cazmatrans bus was in Backa Palanka, a number of individuals burst into the bus, identified themselves as members of the Territorial Defence and they simply requisitioned the bus and it had never been seen again. Since we also had a terrible problem with food, and particularly with medicines, in Ilok, the only person who was brave enough to go to Sid was Ivica Matkovic. He managed to cross the border and he drove a trailer lorry there, filled it with food and medicines, and on the way he was stopped at Sid, sent him to prison, and they confiscated the whole load of truck. That's how life was and how communications were. I think as early as on the 6th of October, Ilok had been receiving electricity from Backa Palanka because all the lines with the Croatian electrical grid were severed. On that day, electricity supply was simply cut off and all lines were practically severed. Fridges were not working. Food was rotting in the fridge. There was no radio transmission. There was no TV broadcast. A few people had transistor radios, but since the relays were also demolished, we could not listen to Radio Zagreb at all. The only radio station that we could listen to was Radio Osijek. However, Belgrade-based radio stations were perfectly audible.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: I'm going to stop you there, please, Mr. Kraljevic. I think you've given --

utterances.speaker: STIPAN KRALJEVIC
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: -- a good idea of the conditions at that time in terms of the refugees and supplies and the electricity. A moment ago, you mentioned that there were persons from the Red Cross who were involved in trying to deal with the situation in Ilok. During this time period, I want to ask you, were there any other persons, representatives from other organisations who were present in Ilok?

utterances.speaker: STIPAN KRALJEVIC
utterances.text: Before the 8th of October, there were no other individuals that could have provided assistance in a humanitarian way. This was something that the citizens themselves organised. When I mentioned the Red Cross, I meant that the population of Ilok held themselves as well, not only rely -- they didn't rely only on the Red Cross. The situation was very serious although I must say that there was a certain level of communication; however, at one point we realised that Ilok was surrounded and that two monitors managed to come to Ilok across the bridge. I am talking about Hugh Cunningham, a Canadian, and Petr Kypr, a monitor from Prague, in Czechoslovakia.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: Mr. Kraljevic, to stop you for a moment, what organisations did these monitors represent?

utterances.speaker: STIPAN KRALJEVIC
utterances.text: I believe that they were European Union monitors, but I don't know exactly. Yes, European monitors. I don't know the exact name of the organisation, really.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: And when these monitors arrived in Ilok, what did you tell them about the situation in terms of the number of people and the difficulties that you've described?

utterances.speaker: STIPAN KRALJEVIC
utterances.text: A few of us, I think there were three or four of us, informed them about the entire situation; however, they were not satisfied with that. They wanted to see for themselves. They went around Ilok. They talked to people, and they could verify everything that we described for them, which is the same as I did for you now. And in that way, they managed to familiarise themselves with the situation in Ilok and the surrounding area.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: I would like for the assistance of the Registrar, please, to pull up 65 ter 00381. This is tab 3. It's a report of the monitors, the European Commission, dated the 9th of October, 1991. Could we have the B/C/S translation as well. And if we could move the B/C/S a bit to the left so we can see the left margin, please. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: Mr. Kraljevic, I would like to you read in the B/C/S, which is on the left-hand side of your screen, points 1 through 5, and then let me know when you're done, please.

utterances.speaker: STIPAN KRALJEVIC
utterances.text: I have finished. May I read it now. Oh, yes, I'm sorry. Number one, Ilok wasn't attacked.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: You can read it to yourself and let me know when you're done reading 1 through 5.

utterances.speaker: STIPAN KRALJEVIC
utterances.text: I've read it.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: Okay. Mr. Kraljevic, we see in this report that the team of monitors, I believe you said you met with a Mr. Cunningham and Mr. Kypr, that they visited Ilok and this report says that -- the report describes the situation in Ilok. And in point 5, do you see where it says that: "Due to the factors which aren't listed above, the whole community is under extreme stress."

utterances.speaker: STIPAN KRALJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: Is this an accurate statement of the situation in Ilok when the monitors arrived?

utterances.speaker: STIPAN KRALJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, even more than that. In a nutshell, this was a description of the prevailing situation.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: At this time, the Prosecution wishes to tender this document into evidence, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It shall be assigned Exhibit Number P2018. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: And we could take that down now, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: Mr. Kraljevic, I want to change topics now and I want to ask you about the negotiations -- may I proceed?

utterances.speaker: STIPAN KRALJEVIC
utterances.text: Please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: I want to ask you about the negotiations that were held in October of 1991 between the negotiating commission comprised of representatives of Ilok and the JNA. My first question is: When did you become involved in negotiations with the JNA?

utterances.speaker: STIPAN KRALJEVIC
utterances.text: I became personally involved on the 7th of October; however, the negotiations with representatives of the Yugoslav Army lasted throughout the whole summer because representatives of the local government, the president and his deputies were maintaining contact, and due to the fact that fields had to be worked and since the army was deployed in the area, we always had to pass through these checkpoints, and that is why the negotiations had been going for so long even before I joined them. At first, a commission was set up made up of a number of people representing all ethnic communities so that the negotiations could be channeled properly and so that always the same persons would be involved. This provided for continuous negotiations, primarily with Colonel Grahovac whose units were stationed in Vojvodina, but also near the bridge in the territory of the town of Ilok.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Kraljevic, can you tell me what position did you hold on this commission?

utterances.speaker: STIPAN KRALJEVIC
utterances.text: At an extended meeting of the city council, a committee or a commission was elected made up of several members. Among them was, for example, Sulejman Salihovic, Josip Cermak, a Slovak by ethnicity. Salihovic was a Muslim by affiliation. Then Lazar Kuljancic, a Serb; Slobodan Savic, a Serb; Maja Samsalovic, who represented women. Then there was Ivan Mrsic. He was the president of the Ilok Assembly. Then villages were represented by Plazonic of Bapska, Rendulic of Lovas, and from Sarengrad, yes, Dr. Holoker from Sarengrad. Well, that would be more or less the composition of this commission. After the commission was set up, we discussed issues at their headquarters in Backa Palanka. It was a long meeting --

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: Mr. Kraljevic, I'm going to ask you to pause for a moment, please. The specific question that I would like for you to answer first is: What was your position on this commission?

utterances.speaker: STIPAN KRALJEVIC
utterances.text: Actually, at that time I was elected chairman of that commission as a senior person. I used to be a teacher in the secondary school, and on the basis of that, they believed me to be a serious and composed person capable of discussing and talking.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm mindful of the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Clanton. Mr. Kraljevic, this is the time for our first break, 30-minute break. We'll come back at 11.00. And the court usher will escort you out of the courtroom. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I may, while the witness is being brought in. During the break, I spoke to Mr. Zivanovic and he's indicated that the Defence does not have an objection to the addition of the two documents that were provided by Mr. Kraljevic yesterday. These were disclosed and then sent through by separate e-mail, and so at this time we would like to ask that they be added to the 65 ter list.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Are they already on your list of documents?

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: They are. They are on the list that we sent through last night.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Being tab numbers?

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: 59. And there's actually a second 59 which should have been a 60.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Two 59s. Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: The 65 ter numbers are 06442 and 06443.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: You may add them to your 65 ter list, to the 65 ter list, Ms. Clanton.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Ms. Clanton.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Kraljevic, before the break we were speaking about the commission that was formed and your position on this commission as the chairman. I would like to ask you, were you aware of negotiations taking place -- I'm sorry, let me withdraw that. You have told us that you were aware of negotiations taking place prior to the time that the commission was formed in October of 1991, and I want to ask you what you heard about who participated in the negotiations prior to October 1991.

utterances.speaker: STIPAN KRALJEVIC
utterances.text: Petar Cobankovic took part in these negotiations. He was the deputy of the president of the local commune of Ilok. Furthermore, there was Ivan Mrsic, who was president of the Assembly of the local commune of Ilok. Then there was Borislav Magovac, who worked at Backa Palanka and knew many people there, including the mayor and others. Then there was Ivan Uros, he was also a member of the Croatian parliament. There were talks about various topics such as working the land and other problems. The most serious problems were also discussed, such as the eviction of population, and the army entering villages and towns. Then the problem of displaced persons at Ilok and problems connected with that.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: Can I stop you there, please. You've told us the persons who attended from Ilok. Can you describe for the Chamber who attended on the other side for these earlier negotiations?

utterances.speaker: STIPAN KRALJEVIC
utterances.text: For the other side, there was always Petar Grahovac, colonel of the Yugoslav army, and the representatives of Backa Palanka were the president of the municipality, as far as I know. And when I was present at the talks at Sid, there was also the deputy of the president of the municipality of Sid. There was also the deputy of the president of the Vukovar Assembly, Mr. Kojic. I'm not sure about his exact position, though.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: Mr. Kraljevic, I'm going to stop you again, please. These earlier negotiations that you've told us you heard about but did not take part in, what was the thing that the JNA wanted from those negotiations?

utterances.speaker: STIPAN KRALJEVIC
utterances.text: The JNA had some main goals. First, for the civil protection to surrender all their weapons. Secondly, they wanted the army to be let into the populated places and search them. They also wanted to apply sanctions to the people who had caused tensions or committed crimes in those areas. They simply wanted to enter the town and impose military rule.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: Mr. Kraljevic, what month were these negotiations held, these negotiations that you were not part of?

utterances.speaker: STIPAN KRALJEVIC
utterances.text: The talks at Sid took place on the 30th of September. There were other talks in early October, but there were other talks even before. This would be it in a nutshell.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: Okay. Now I'd like to ask you about the talks that you participated in. You've told us that there were talks in Backa Palanka and that there was an officer of the Yugoslav army named Colonel Grahovac who was involved in those talks. Can you tell us what Colonel Grahovac said would happen if the wishes of the JNA were not respected?

utterances.speaker: STIPAN KRALJEVIC
utterances.text: The JNA demanded what I have just stated. Unless their demands were met, that is the weapons, which were light weapons, rifles, possession of the civil protection, they were to be surrendered by the bridge at the Zec workshop and controlled by the army. They also wanted to be allowed to take the city. Otherwise, they would use all their firepower to make it happen.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: And what did Colonel Grahovac say about the events that could take place in Ilok compared to what was taking place in Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: STIPAN KRALJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. He said that their actions would be such that the combat wouldn't go on for days, but given the imbalance of power, it would all be over within hours. And that was a realistic expectation given the imbalance of power.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: Now, other than Colonel Grahovac, who else did you meet with from the JNA?

utterances.speaker: STIPAN KRALJEVIC
utterances.text: Colonel Tomic also attended the meetings regularly. Our negotiating committee representing the town of Ilok said that we couldn't yield to their demands because we didn't have the authority to take such decisions. We were willing to disarm the civil protection but wanted to store the weapons at the depot of the Ilok police. Furthermore, there was no legal or constitutional provision allowing the army to enter Ilok and keep law and order there. That was for the MUP, that is, the police, to do.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: Mr. Kraljevic, I'm going to pause you again and ask you, you've given us the names of Colonel Grahovac and Colonel Tomic. Were there any other officers of the JNA who you remember meeting with?

utterances.speaker: STIPAN KRALJEVIC
utterances.text: Not up until the 11th of October. But General Dragoljub Arandjelovic was Colonel Grahovac's superior, and the latter said that that was the man to talk to about possible solutions to this crisis. And he suggested that we go to Sid to speak to General Arandjelovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: At this time I would like the Registrar's assistance. If we could please pull up 65 ter 05030.6. This is a video-clip that comes from the video which has ERN V0004590, and in the packet it's at tab 29. This is a news report, and I would like to play it without the sound and I only want to play a part of it. And after we play it once through, we'll go back and pause at a certain point, please. If we could get it ready to play, please, from 34 minutes and 3 seconds to 34 minutes and 30 seconds.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Kraljevic, were you able to see the image on the screen in front of you?

utterances.speaker: STIPAN KRALJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: Do you recognise either of the men who appear in this video-clip?

utterances.speaker: STIPAN KRALJEVIC
utterances.text: I see one man and that's General Arandjelovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: At this time we'd like to tender this still, which has a separate 65 ter number. It's at 34 minutes and 30 seconds, and that 65 ter is 05030.10.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Ms. Clanton, is that a clip or the photograph of this man -- the image of this man?

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: I would like to tender the image, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: The image. Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It shall be assigned Exhibit Number P2019. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: And I saw the witness change his glasses so he probably did not see the beginning of the clip where the other man appeared. I don't know if it is of any importance to you but just telling you.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: I think since he's identified the person who is at the still at the time code where the video was paused, I'm comfortable with his identification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: Mr. Kraljevic, a moment ago you told us about the demands of the JNA, and you stated that the position of the commission was that they would not be able to agree to those including the surrender of weapons. I'd like to know if you ever provided an alternative peace proposal to the JNA?

utterances.speaker: STIPAN KRALJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I was going to say that, that we put forward an alternative proposal, namely for the civil protection to be disarmed and all their weapons to be placed at the police station so that the police may do their work. Because there were no conflicts, no clashes among the population of the town or in the surrounding villages. There's never been -- there had never been one incident justifying an intervention from outside.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: Mr. Kraljevic, I want to ask you, please, were you able to give your alternative proposal to General Arandjelovic?

utterances.speaker: STIPAN KRALJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, we were. We gave them our proposal but they never even looked at it. General Arandjelovic made his own proposal which was actually an ultimatum for the surrender of the weapons. It had a number of articles and he demanded that we sign it immediately. We replied that we couldn't do that because it was for the citizens to decide about that in a referendum. Our committee didn't have the authority to make such a decision.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: Mr. Kraljevic, the ultimatum that was given to you, to your committee by General Arandjelovic, what did it say about the surrender of weapons?

utterances.speaker: STIPAN KRALJEVIC
utterances.text: In that article or that provision of the agreement, which was an ultimatum, stated that all the weapons had to be surrendered by 12.00 noon on the following day. The place where that should be done was the workshop of Ivan Zec controlled by the JNA. If that wasn't done, the army would enter the town and fulfill their task.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: I would like the Registrar to please pull up 65 ter 00403, which is Prosecution Exhibit 318. This is at tab 6.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: Mr. Kraljevic, do you recognise this as a document that you provided to investigators of the OTP?

utterances.speaker: STIPAN KRALJEVIC
utterances.text: On the right side, no. On one side, there is the agreement issued by the Yugoslav army, and on the other side there's something in English. Oh, must be the English translation. This is the agreement as proposed by Arandjelovic on the 12th of October.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: I would like to ask you to look at clause 1, please. It says that all weapons should be surrendered to the JNA, in particular to the members of the 1st Military District.

utterances.speaker: STIPAN KRALJEVIC
utterances.text: Regardless of how they were obtained, to the military police of the 1st Military District, safe access to Ilok, and a search of all private, social and state facilities --

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: Sir, if I could ask you to pause, please. I didn't intend for you to read it. If you could now look at clause 7, please. Here it says that if weapons are used or if the security of the JNA is threatened, retaliatory measures are authorised. I want to ask you what kind of retaliatory measures did you think could happen?

utterances.speaker: STIPAN KRALJEVIC
utterances.text: First of all, there was never any threat to the security of JNA members, nor was that possible in practice. But retaliatory measures is a phrase that we understood implying everything that had already been happening in all those villages, that houses would be entered, that people would be killed, that there would be no law and order, which would allow individuals to commit crimes, atrocities, beatings. So that was what we could expect. It had happened at Bapska, Tovarnik, Lovas before, basically everywhere where the units had entered.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: Mr. Kraljevic, you told us that when this ultimatum was put to you, the members of the negotiating commission could not agree to it and that they had to go back and speak to the people. Now, before the meeting ended with General Arandjelovic, do you remember if the members of the commission asked any questions to General Arandjelovic?

utterances.speaker: STIPAN KRALJEVIC
utterances.text: It was a long conversation because there was a number of people there, the entire committee, practically, and I mentioned the names already. For example, Mr. Mato Brletic, the Ilok police commander, told the General that there were over 10.000 people at Ilok and asked him if he wasn't sorry because there would have to be casualties. Arandjelovic replied: "I'm a soldier and I will do what I'm told, that is take the territory." On the 10th, the previous day, at Lovas, over 20 people, actually 22 to be precise, which figure I learned later from the European monitors, had been killed. Mr. Rendulic asked why so many people had been killed at Lovas. The General replied it had been done in retaliation for the death of a soldier whose body was found in a cornfield. But there was no body found in a cornfield. Nobody ever proved that. This was a clear indication of what we could expect if the units were to enter town.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: Now, I want to ask you about what was happening amongst the community leaders of Ilok at this time, so after you finished your meeting with General Arandjelovic when he delivered this ultimatum, I want to know if you recall that there were discussions among the community representatives about what had happened during those negotiations?

utterances.speaker: STIPAN KRALJEVIC
utterances.text: Representatives of Sarengrad -- excuse me, Bapska, given the fact that the majority of Bapska residents were in Ilok, asked Arandjelovic to go to Bapska in order to collect some of their belongings, at least the basic ones --

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: If I could ask you to pause for a moment. The question that I've asked you actually pertains to what was happening in Ilok at the time, if there were any meetings among people in Ilok about what had happened during the negotiations.

utterances.speaker: STIPAN KRALJEVIC
utterances.text: All I wanted to say was to describe what was still happening in the meeting of the 11th, when General Arandjelovic issued a few passes to citizens allowing them to go to Bapska and gather their things. I'm sorry, I'll finish very soon.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: Can I just ask you to pause there because we will come to these topics, but for right now, I want to ask you about when you went back to Ilok. Were there meetings of any community group to discuss what had happened in the negotiations?

utterances.speaker: STIPAN KRALJEVIC
utterances.text: Well, I believe that our commission conveyed all the information to the citizens. It typically happened in the culture hall where a huge crowd of citizens were present, not only representatives of the authorities from Bapska, Lovas and other places. Everybody was interested to know what was going on. We informed them about the negotiations because the majority of residents wanted to protect their own lives. We also discussed the issue of evacuation of the population so as to see how to deal with things for at least a certain period of time until the issues have been resolved. You are probably aware that at the time, there were intense intergovernmental talks at the highest level between Mr. Tudjman and Mr. Milosevic, and at the time, we expected a certain agreement to be reached which would calm the situation. Now, there were constant agreements being signed about cease-fire but cease-fire never happened. So there were negotiations going on a daily basis, but the point was that nobody was willing to leave their place of residence and that was the main point. When we talked to the citizens, we told them --

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: Mr. Kraljevic, what I want focus on is what you just said, that you were part of the group that talked to the citizens and that these questions about solutions at a national level and also about what would happen in Ilok were being raised and addressed in your community, which you've just told us.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: I would like to ask for the Registrar to please bring up 65 ter 00214, which is Prosecution Exhibit 321. This is at tab 23, and these are the minutes of the Ilok urban community Assembly from this time period in 1991.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Kraljevic, since you arrived here in The Hague, have you had an opportunity to read the minutes of the Ilok community Assembly which are in front of you on the left-hand side of your screen?

utterances.speaker: STIPAN KRALJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: If we could please scroll down to the last page, I think it's page 5.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Kraljevic, do you recognise the signature at the bottom right of this page?

utterances.speaker: STIPAN KRALJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: Whose signature is it?

utterances.speaker: STIPAN KRALJEVIC
utterances.text: It's my signature.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: And do you recognise the name or the signature that's at the bottom left of the page?

utterances.speaker: STIPAN KRALJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, Nevenka Brkic, note-taker of the Ilok town government. I recognise her signature.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Kraljevic, since you've had an opportunity to read these minutes, can you confirm that the minutes are a true and accurate reflection of the discussions of the community leaders in Ilok at this time?

utterances.speaker: STIPAN KRALJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Sorry, if we can have clarification what does it mean "at this time"?

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: If I may, Your Honour, I was referring to the dates that are in the minutes which span from the 6th of October to the 16th of October, 1991.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Does that satisfy you, Mr. Zivanovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: And we can take that down now.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: Mr. Kraljevic, I would like now to turn back to what you were telling me about a moment ago, which was the events that led to the organisation of a referendum on the 13th of October, 1991. As you've explained, this was a referendum for the community related to the ultimatum that we were just talking about. Can you tell me how many questions were put to the people in Ilok in this referendum?

utterances.speaker: STIPAN KRALJEVIC
utterances.text: The referendum was called to be held on the Sunday and there were two questions on ballot papers -- or actually, there were two types of ballot papers. One contained the question whether you are in favour of handing over the weapons to the JNA and to allow the entry -- I'm sorry, it was not in the question. The question was only relating to the handing over of the weapons to the JNA. Attached to this ballot paper and displayed at polling stations and every public places, an ultimatum that had been submitted to us on the 11th of October by the JNA during the talks in Sid, and there was another ballot paper asking the citizens to say whether they were in favour of evacuation or migration of the population in the event of a crisis emerging, by which we meant an attack by the army and their entering Ilok. Because they explicitly said either the weapons and the entry into Ilok or any further negotiations will be suspended.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: Now if the Registrar could please assist by pulling up 65 ter 00404, which is Prosecution Exhibit 319. This is at tab 7.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: Mr. Kraljevic, do you recognise the document on the left as a document that you provided to the investigators at the OTP?

utterances.speaker: STIPAN KRALJEVIC
utterances.text: I and my colleagues drafted the wording of this paper. In the first one -- I don't need to read it; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: That's correct. Do you recognise this as a document that you provided to the investigators of the Office of the Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: STIPAN KRALJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: If we could please have now 65 ter 06442.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: Mr. Kraljevic, do you recognise the document front of you as a document you provided to the Office of the Prosecutor yesterday?

utterances.speaker: STIPAN KRALJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: And can you explain, in the first line where it's handwritten and says "veterinary," what does this place name refer to?

utterances.speaker: STIPAN KRALJEVIC
utterances.text: That's a veterinary station in Ilok. It's located on Radiceva Street, on the road from the centre of Ilok towards Sid. There were five such polling stations and the citizens could vote at these places.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: Mr. Kraljevic, is it correct that the names of the polling stations appear on each of the pages that you gave to us yesterday? At the top of the page.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: If the Registrar could briefly scroll down --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: Actually, it's okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Kraljevic, you've told us that these documents record the place where the people were voting. What I now want to ask you is if the numbers on the documents reflect the numbers of votes that were cast?

utterances.speaker: STIPAN KRALJEVIC
utterances.text: You will see the signatures of the members of the committee which confirm this. There is also a final report, an aggregate report from all polling stations.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: Before we get --

utterances.speaker: STIPAN KRALJEVIC
utterances.text: Therefore, the guarantee is provided by the signatures we see here. I don't need to give you any further guarantees.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: Before we get to the aggregate document that you've mentioned, I want you to explain. On the page that's in front of you, about two-thirds of the way down the page where it says there are 508 ballots reflecting the wishes of 1059 citizens. Can you briefly tell the Trial Chamber why those numbers are different?

utterances.speaker: STIPAN KRALJEVIC
utterances.text: The number of ballot papers where the word "for" was 508 --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please repeat the figures once again. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: Mr. Kraljevic, excuse me. The interpreter would like for you to please repeat what you just said about the figures.

utterances.speaker: STIPAN KRALJEVIC
utterances.text: The 508 people encircled the word "for," and at the bottom you see the figure 1059, which includes their family members including children who were ready to move out. So that means that they voted for -- on behalf of all members of their families because children cannot vote. Or, for example, a wife would vote on behalf of both her husband and children. I hope I was clear.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: Yes. At this time we would like to have this document, 06442, admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It should be assigned Exhibit Number P2020. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: And if the Registrar could assist by please bringing up 06443. This is the second document that was provided by the witness yesterday, and it's at the second tab 59 which should be tab 60.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: Mr. Kraljevic, a moment ago you mentioned that there was a table that has the aggregate results from the various polling stations. Is this the table that you're referring to?

utterances.speaker: STIPAN KRALJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: And there's a Roman numeral 1 and there's a Roman numeral 2. Can you briefly explain what Roman numeral 1 reflects and then what Roman numeral 2 reflects?

utterances.speaker: STIPAN KRALJEVIC
utterances.text: Under Roman numeral number 1 is the results of the voting on the handing over of weapons and signing the agreements. The total against were 71 per cent or 2519 people constitutes the number of turnout. And the second ballot paper contains votes of people in the event of a crisis emerging. I think that the total number is, if I see correctly, 2577, which means that 73 per cent were for and 11 per cent were against. Totalling 497 people.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: At this time we would seek to have this document, 65 ter 06443, be admitted into evidence, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It should be assigned Exhibit Number P2021. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Kraljevic, you've just told us the results of the referendum that was held on the 13th of October, 1991. I want to ask you, how did you convey the results of the referendum to the JNA?

utterances.speaker: STIPAN KRALJEVIC
utterances.text: The referendum was held on Sunday, the 13th of October. Before that, in the meeting with General Arandjelovic on the 11th, we agreed that after the referendum he would be given all the results on the Monday at 12.00, that is to say, on the 14th of October. Prior to that, we had a session of the town council and we informed all the citizens who were present about the results, at least those who were at the culture hall at 9.00. And then at 12.00, we were in Sid where we went to see General Arandjelovic to inform him about the results of the referendum.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: And was there anyone else present at the negotiations other than the people who were part of your negotiating commission and General Arandjelovic?

utterances.speaker: STIPAN KRALJEVIC
utterances.text: This meeting where information was conveyed was attended by two ECMM members, namely Hugh Cunningham and Petr Kypr. The two were a bit late in arriving at the meeting, but practically, they did attend the entire duration of the meeting.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: And can you describe for us what happened at this meeting?

utterances.speaker: STIPAN KRALJEVIC
utterances.text: To put it simply, as the chairman of the committee, I informed the General about the decision of the Assembly and the outcome of the referendum. He only said, "Well, that's how you decided," and he suggested that we draw up an agreement on the migration of people from the town.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: And what did this agreement say?

utterances.speaker: STIPAN KRALJEVIC
utterances.text: I think that this agreement had several clauses, a dozen or so, I don't know exactly. It says that if citizens want to leave and move out -- although when any such notes were made, we lodged protests, it wasn't acceptable. Quite simply, this agreement was simply dictated by the Sid Municipal Assembly to the typist secretary who was also present at the meeting. Mr. Brletic and I were present while this agreement was being dictated to the typist, but we didn't have any room to exert any influence on the contents and conclusion of such an agreement. At the very meeting, we underlined, and we did the same in the presence of the observers, that we didn't want to leave Ilok because that meant that we would have to leave everything behind, and we were wondering about what our prospects were, how people would return and everything was an unknown. We had no place to go. It's very difficult to leave your home and go to an unknown place where you don't know anyone. And the observers also wanted to hear that. But there was one request that was permanently repeated and that is that the JNA must enter the town, must take and confiscate the arms, and must search all the facilities, and if they find someone with hidden weapons, they would take measures. In a nutshell, there was no other way out so we had to sign this agreement.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: I would like the assistance of the Registrar, please, to pull up Prosecution Exhibit 1419, which is 65 ter 5057. This is at tab 36.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: Mr. Kraljevic, do you recognise this document?

utterances.speaker: STIPAN KRALJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: If we could go to the last page, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: Whose signature is on the bottom -- I'm sorry, on the left side?

utterances.speaker: STIPAN KRALJEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Ivan Mrsic.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: And on the right side?

utterances.speaker: STIPAN KRALJEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Dragoljub Arandjelovic, the General, and commander of the area on behalf of the Yugoslav Army.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: Mr. Kraljevic, just so that the record is clear, do you recognise this as the document that was signed on October 14th, 1991, that we've been discussing?

utterances.speaker: STIPAN KRALJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: Now, after this agreement was signed, did any of the people who were representing Ilok, any of the people who came as part of the commission, did they have any requests to make or any statements related to how they were going to be able to leave?

utterances.speaker: STIPAN KRALJEVIC
utterances.text: Well, everybody was just saying that they didn't want to leave, but that the army should show at least some degree of benevolence and allow the residents to stay in their home and not move out.
