However, their position was very firm and there was no way of influencing it. For that reason, the citizens requested at least to be provided with some degree of safety while they were leaving the area, to be allowed to take some of their possessions with them, and these provisions were entered into the agreement. So in short, that would be it, and these requests were approved.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: Earlier when we were discussing negotiations, you mentioned that there were people who were part of this commission who were representatives from Bapska and that they wished to be able to gather their belongings. Do you recall that any of the people from Bapska were making this request during this meeting?

utterances.speaker: STIPAN KRALJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. There was Mr. Ivan Sablic, he also requested permits. The General issued passes, and some residents of Bapska went from Ilok to Bapska to gather their belongings. But you see, once they received Bapska, they were thinking of taking a shortcut towards Sid. Although they had the passes, they were stopped on the way. Some of them ended up in the Begejci camp, some were detained in Sid, I think in a sports hall. And some ended in the Begejci camp, including Mr. Sablic, and I think that he was exchanged sometime around the 15th of December, 1991.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: I'd like for the Registrar's assistance to please pull up 65 ter 00438, which is at tab 14.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: Mr. Kraljevic, do you recognise this list?

utterances.speaker: STIPAN KRALJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: Do you recognise the signature?

utterances.speaker: STIPAN KRALJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: Whose signature is it?

utterances.speaker: STIPAN KRALJEVIC
utterances.text: Mine.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: And I would like for you to look at this list and tell me if any of the people who are on this list were part of the group that you've described that sought to have permits to go back to Bapska and gather their belongings.

utterances.speaker: STIPAN KRALJEVIC
utterances.text: Miroslav Kolak, Nada Vrbanic, Ivan Mijic, that is number 11, 7, and 3. They were in a passenger car accompanied by another person. When they were leaving Bapska, fire was opened at them without any warning. Mijic was wounded, but survived.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: Mr. Kraljevic, are you saying that it is not correct where it says that Mijic was killed in Bapska on Bracka Radic Street on the 14th of October, 1991? This is number 11.

utterances.speaker: STIPAN KRALJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Killed on the 14th of October in Bapska by the JNA on Bracka Radic Street. We can even see the name of the street here.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: Is it correct that he was killed in this way on the 14th of October, 1991, on the street Bracka Radic Street?

utterances.speaker: STIPAN KRALJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: At this time, Your Honours, we'd like to tender 65 ter 00438 into evidence, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Should be assigned Exhibit Number P2022. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: Mr. Kraljevic, now I want to talk to you about your departure from Ilok on the 17th of October, 1991. As you were preparing for the departure on that day, can you describe the atmosphere in Ilok?

utterances.speaker: STIPAN KRALJEVIC
utterances.text: First of all, after the signing of this agreement, we organised for the population to be informed about this agreement and their options. The citizens understood they didn't need much explanation of the situation at Ilok because they could see it for themselves. We just told them that it was up to them to decide what to do because a date had been set and it had been set with the representatives of the JNA, but the evacuation of the population could be done in various ways. They could either leave towards Backa Palanka and Nestin, which is in Vojvodina, that is Serbia, or through Sot, Sid, Adasevac, Lipovac, to Croatia. They could either stay or leave in one of these ways. And the situation itself, I don't know what to say about it. The citizens were informed. They could decide for themselves. We couldn't and wouldn't guarantee that they would fare better if they stayed or left. We didn't know whether anybody would stop them during their departure. We couldn't give any guarantees. The guarantees were given by the army according to the agreement. That would be it in short.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: During this time period, what kinds of noises or sounds could you hear in Ilok?

utterances.speaker: STIPAN KRALJEVIC
utterances.text: First of all, at that time there was still heavy shelling in Vukovar. There were detonations all the time, aircraft flying over Ilok. And at Principovac, where the JNA units were, there were very strong loudspeakers from which you could often hear folk music with offensive lyrics. Often there was shooting from machine-guns that could be heard on the streets of Ilok. That was the situation.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: And during this time, what preparations were made in respect of certain items of the cultural heritage of Ilok?

utterances.speaker: STIPAN KRALJEVIC
utterances.text: We spoke about that to Colonel Grahovac. We wanted to evacuate the most important exhibits from the museum because the museum belonged to the population of the town, the inhabitants, so if the inhabitants are leaving, we also wanted to preserve those unique exhibits. They were indeed packed by the museum staff, but at the last moment, an order came in that nothing could be taken away. I can add now that most exhibits have been preserved. During the occupation, one staff member stayed throughout that period and some others also stayed, but the most valuable 22 paintings disappeared. They were cut out from their frames and taken away.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: Mr. Kraljevic, I would like to go back for one moment, please. You answered a question that I asked and told me about songs that were being played from speakers from where the JNA was at Principovac and you described the lyrics as offensive. Can you tell me what was offensive about the lyrics, what were they saying that was offensive?

utterances.speaker: STIPAN KRALJEVIC
utterances.text: There were all kinds of lyrics. It's better not to go into that. We know what it was about. Three more days only and then there will be -- those things, I really wouldn't speak about it. Everybody understood anyway. Various things had happened even before. People were arrested and taken away --

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: If I ask you to pause, please. I know that you understand why the lyrics were offensive, but for the benefit of everyone in the courtroom, would you please tell us who they were offensive to or in what way they were offensive?

utterances.speaker: STIPAN KRALJEVIC
utterances.text: Well, if there is talk about slaughter, then it is offensive, of course. There are various kinds of songs, songs saying that -- or, rather, expressing no good wishes to the population.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: Mr. Kraljevic, these songs that you've now described, in the lyrics, who is being slaughtered?

utterances.speaker: STIPAN KRALJEVIC
utterances.text: Who is being slaughtered? Well, you know, it's a campaign of fear. It didn't mean that it would really happen but it's good for instilling fear in people. But it's certainly true that during the war all sorts of things happened.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: Mr. Kraljevic, you've now said that these lyrics had the effect of instilling fear even if the threat was not actually carried out in terms of an actual slaughter event. What I'm interested in finding out is who felt fear, who felt threatened?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Sorry, may we have clarification was it lyrics, poems, poetry or songs?

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I understood from the translation that he was referring to the lyrics in a song. If you would like for me to clarify with the witness, I can do that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The songs that were being sung, that's what I'm talking about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: It's already in the answer, I think, at --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The songs that were sung.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: And, Mr. Kraljevic, to go back to my question on this, you've said that the lyrics of these songs and the playing of these songs had the effect of instilling fear in people. Was there a group of people who the songs had the effect of instilling fear in them?

utterances.speaker: STIPAN KRALJEVIC
utterances.text: Members of the civil protection were especially frightened but also the members of the Croatian Democratic Union, the HDZ, because there were always threats to the HDZ, but also to the civil protection and anybody who had any sort of weapon or some such.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm mindful of the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Ms. Clanton. Mr. Kraljevic, this is the time for our second break for half an hour as well. So we will come back at 12.45. The court usher will escort you out of the courtroom. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Please go ahead, Ms. Clanton.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: Mr. Kraljevic, before we took the break, we were talking about the departure of the people from Ilok on October 17th, 1991. Can you tell the Chamber, briefly, what time the convoy was supposed to leave?

utterances.speaker: STIPAN KRALJEVIC
utterances.text: On the 17th starting at 7.00 and as long as was necessary for everybody to leave. It meant that the people who wanted to leave with their property on trailers and vans, or whatever vehicles, formed a convoy which then set off. Before that, according to the agreement, the police had to collect the weapons and hand them over to the JNA by the bridge. That was done. As far as I know, it must have been at 7.00. The police did that. I am not familiar with the details of the process.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: Mr. Kraljevic, I'm going to pause you there. I would like to know now, where were the people who were leaving Ilok supposed to gather?

utterances.speaker: STIPAN KRALJEVIC
utterances.text: They gathered to form a convoy toward the bridge. I don't know how to describe it. It's the main street from -- it leads from Ilok to Backa Palanka and Nestin. That street was packed. But the side streets were also full of displaced persons. Some people were simply in front of their houses, and that convoy slowly moved all day.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: And, Mr. Kraljevic, who was in charge of processing the people in the column, the people and the vehicles in the column?

utterances.speaker: STIPAN KRALJEVIC
utterances.text: It was said by way of informing the people and the people themselves. The column moved slowly. There were also some monitors, they were four of them at the time, and they were going up and down the column. That's what the police did also. But it was an orderly process, and about half a day -- it took half a day to get from Ilok to the checkpoint.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: Mr. Kraljevic, when you got to the checkpoint, who was at the checkpoint?

utterances.speaker: STIPAN KRALJEVIC
utterances.text: There were people in JNA uniforms, nobody I knew. There were a few people in uniforms who were from Ilok, but it doesn't matter.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: I'd like Mr. Laugel to please assist by playing a video-clip. It's actually two video-clips and I'd like to play them back to back. The first one is very short. It's 65 ter 04929.4. And this comes from the video with ERN V0003949. If you could just wait one moment, Thomas. He is going to play from 7.05 to 7.58.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: And I want to make sure that, Mr. Kraljevic, if you need to switch your glasses to able to see the screen, please do so.

utterances.speaker: STIPAN KRALJEVIC
utterances.text: I can see well enough with these. As long as there's no need to read.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: We're not going to play the sound on this. It's only for the images, and I want to warn the Chamber that the quality of this video is not very good. We're only going to play a short part, but it will freeze in certain parts but it will pick back up.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: And now I would like for Mr. Laugel to play the video that has 65 ter number 05016.2. This would be starting at 31 minutes, 15 seconds to 32 minutes and 20 seconds. I would also like for this one to be played without the sound. I should have said the previous video was at tab 56. This one is at tab 57.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Kraljevic, I would like to ask you, do you recognise the town where this footage was taken?

utterances.speaker: STIPAN KRALJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, there are two situations. One is at Ilok, one of the columns. You can tell by the checkpoints at the points of exit. There are many sandbags and there were many soldiers watching the column leave Ilok. There is also a still of the column at Ilok itself. Some of it was taken at Sarengrad. I saw the Orthodox church there.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: Mr. Kraljevic, if I could ask you to pause, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: I think this was the part of the video that we were not intending to show, but if it would assist the Court, we could have the witness identify that part. I was interested in the footage that he's already described. It was just a technical thing when we started the clip that it started a bit early.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: It's your call. Go on, Ms. Clanton.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: Mr. Kraljevic, the footage of the people and the convoy and soldiers at the checkpoints, are you informing us with your previous answer that this is all footage that was from Ilok?

utterances.speaker: STIPAN KRALJEVIC
utterances.text: Apart from what I said about Sarengrad, yes. Although I cannot be sure of some of the footage. It seems that some of it was not taken at Ilok, but this was.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: Mr. Kraljevic, the footage you've described of the convoy of people and the checkpoint and the soldiers and the roads that you've identified are in Ilok, does this footage match what you saw and experienced on the 17th of October, 1991?

utterances.speaker: STIPAN KRALJEVIC
utterances.text: Well, yes. I was in that column very long -- it was a very long column. I was part of it. I know what it all looked like. It was a beautiful day. People moved about, talked in groups --

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: Mr. Kraljevic, if I could pause you. I'm sorry, we have limited time.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: At this time I would like to have the video-clips, 04929.4 and 05016.2, admitted into evidence. There are no transcripts, it's only for the images. Your Honour, I had asked that the two video-clips be admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I missed that, Ms. Clanton. Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: They should be assigned Exhibit Numbers P2023 and P2024 respectively. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: Mr. Kraljevic, I want to ask you if all the persons who tried to leave Ilok in the convoy on the 17th of October were able to leave in the convoy?

utterances.speaker: STIPAN KRALJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. They were supposed to leave because an order came on the last day that, according to Mr. Grahovac, even the most hardened criminals are free to leave with the column provided they wished to do so. That was apparently a decision reached at a higher level, but I was not interested in that. But I have to say that 17 people were singled out and taken away from the convoy. The check-ups involved the checking of identification cards and those who were doing the checking were comparing the data with some lists, and they singled out the 17 people I mentioned. I myself did not see it. I may have been in the front of the column or in the back, but we received information that 17 people were taken out of the column. Most of them, except for two or three who were wounded and taken to hospital, ended up in the Begejci camp.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: Mr. Kraljevic, you've explained that you did not see this. It was not in the part of the column where you were at that time, but if you know, can you tell us who pulled these people, these 17 people aside?

utterances.speaker: STIPAN KRALJEVIC
utterances.text: Well, the checkpoints were manned by the representatives of the army and that is what they did. Whether there were any paramilitary troops with them, I cannot tell. Some people had been seen around, but it's not relevant.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: If I could ask the Registrar to assist by pulling up 02215, 65 ter 02215. This is a list of persons separated from the convoy. It's at tab 24.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Kraljevic, do you recognise this list?

utterances.speaker: STIPAN KRALJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: Who prepared this list?

utterances.speaker: STIPAN KRALJEVIC
utterances.text: On the basis of various pieces of information while I was working at the government in Zagreb, people came and provided information with regards to those who were separated, but I received information from other sources and other individuals as well, but I cannot tell you exactly. Anyway, these 17 people were singled out on that occasion and taken out of the convoy.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: Mr. Kraljevic, a moment ago you told us that you believed that, other than two or three persons who had been wounded, that many of these people on the list were taken to the Begejci camp. Can you confirm that this is the list with those people you're referring to?

utterances.speaker: STIPAN KRALJEVIC
utterances.text: Are you referring to the ones that were taken to the hospital because they were wounded?

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: I'm asking you to confirm that a moment ago when you said that people who were taken out of the convoy were taken to Begejci, that this list contains the names of some of those people?

utterances.speaker: STIPAN KRALJEVIC
utterances.text: With the exception of two, all of them.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: At this time, Your Honours, I would like to have 65 ter 02215 admitted into evidence, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It should be assigned Exhibit Number P2025. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Kraljevic, I want to move on to a new topic and that is what you learned about the situation in Ilok after the time that you had left Ilok. Now, while you were mayor of Ilok in exile in Zagreb, can you tell us how you collected information about the situation in Ilok, in particular related to the people who were still there?

utterances.speaker: STIPAN KRALJEVIC
utterances.text: I can tell you that in the town of Ilok itself, there remained probably approximately 1300 inhabitants that we might say were representative of the Croatian community. The majority of Slovaks, if they left at all, went towards Backa Palanka, which is quite understandable because they had large families in Vojvodina. As a rule, they came back very soon thereafter.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: Mr. Kraljevic, sorry, I need to ask you to pause, please. The question that I asked you relates to when you were serving as mayor. How did you get information about what was happening to the people who had stayed behind in Ilok?

utterances.speaker: STIPAN KRALJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I'm sorry. All I wanted to say was that there were people who stayed behind in Ilok who were later expelled. And those who were not expelled managed to go via Vojvodina to Hungary, and then across the border between Hungary and Croatia, they would reach Zagreb, and it is from them that we received information. Some people used telephones provided by the International Community. There were various ways of communication, but the information was mostly provided by the people who managed to cross the border, especially after these expulsions.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: Mr. Kraljevic, you've just mentioned expulsions taking place in Ilok after the time that you left. Do you know who caused people to be expelled from Ilok?

utterances.speaker: STIPAN KRALJEVIC
utterances.text: According to the statements given by the individuals coming from the area, the situation was somewhat peaceful while Colonel Grahovac was in Ilok. He was in charge of maintaining law and order in the town itself and it seems that that was the situation then. However, he left the area in January, late January, he left his position, and practically the command of the town was taken over by the police and the local self-government, and this is particularly a time that was very difficult. But also in the period immediately after our departure, and this was reflected in people being brought into the police premises, being interrogated, and a huge number of people were expelled.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: Mr. Kraljevic, you've told us about two time periods here. You've said immediately after -- or in the months after the column left that people were taken into police stations and mistreated. And then, if I understand correctly, you've told us that after Colonel Grahovac left the area, you said it was a very difficult situation. Can you elaborate a bit more about what you know about it being a very difficult situation?

utterances.speaker: STIPAN KRALJEVIC
utterances.text: The houses that were vacated were being plundered. People used to come from other areas as well, various individuals who were looting the town. Soon thereafter, people started moving into the houses. There were refugees from western Croatia in Backa Palanka and they started moving into those houses in an organised manner. The keys to the houses, if they were left at all, were left with neighbours. If it was impossible to open the door, then they were forced opened. But people were moving out and, as far as I can tell, it was done in a rather organised way. Some people may not have been very happy and they started looking for better houses, especially if there were elderly people living alone in those houses, and they were subjected to maltreatment in order to drive them out of their houses and to move somebody else into them.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: Mr. Kraljevic, you've told us about people being mistreated by the police and then also as part of this -- what you've said was an organised system to remove people from their homes. I want to ask you, who did you hear was operating in Ilok at this time and involved in the commission of these crimes?

utterances.speaker: STIPAN KRALJEVIC
utterances.text: Are you referring to the authorities or what? I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: I'm asking you who you believe -- who you heard was responsible for the crimes that were committed against civilians who remained in Ilok?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Sorry --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: -- may we have the reference where the witness said that people being mistreated by the police.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: If you just give me one moment, Your Honour. Your Honour, on page 31 of the -- oh, I'm sorry. It just moved. 31 of the temporary transcript at lines 11 to 13.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Sorry, it states that people being brought into the police premises, not being mistreated.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: What I see is that it says they were brought into the police premises and being interrogated and a huge number of people were expelled. Would it assist for me to ask the question -- a different question to the witness?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: As long as you don't give the qualification of mistreatment if the -- if the witness doesn't. So you could ask him.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: Mr. Kraljevic, a moment ago, you said to us and I'm going to read this from the transcript because it's important what is recorded, you said that: "... people were brought into police premises, were being interrogated, and a huge number of people were expelled." Could you describe for us what you heard about the way that they were interrogated and who was interrogating them?

utterances.speaker: STIPAN KRALJEVIC
utterances.text: You know, it's difficult for me to say something explicitly in such a way. The people who were brought in know best what happened to them. There are quite a few statements provided by such individuals. I myself didn't collect them, but if necessary, we can review them because there is a multitude of persons who provided statements to that effect. I am reluctant to make any comments in their name.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: Mr. Kraljevic, based on what you heard from these people, can you answer the question that I asked you, which was: Who was interrogating them and what you heard about the interrogations?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: It was asked and answered.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't -- I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: I don't agree, Mr. Zivanovic. It was asked but it wasn't answered.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: In the quoted part of the transcript it was said that they were interrogated in police premises.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: But that's no answer to the question. Please proceed, Ms. Clanton.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: Mr. Kraljevic, I said a moment ago, I need for you to focus on my question, which is: Based on what you heard, who interrogated people in the police premises and what did you hear about the interrogations themselves?

utterances.speaker: STIPAN KRALJEVIC
utterances.text: It is true that people were questioned on the police premises. They were held captive in the cellar and they were maltreated. A lot of people can confirm that, if necessary. But at this point in time, I find it difficult to collect as many people who can testify to that, but it is beyond doubt that people were maltreated, severely maltreated.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: Mr. Kraljevic, if you know, by whom were they severely maltreated when they were detained or held captive in the cellar of the police premises?

utterances.speaker: STIPAN KRALJEVIC
utterances.text: Well, the police. Who else? I don't know. If anyone else was granted access to the police, then it's the police's mistake.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: Mr. Kraljevic, I'd like to go back to the question now that I was asking you before and I think I should ask you again. I want to know, who did you hear, other than the police, who did you hear was operating near Ilok and was responsible for the commission of crimes after the time that you left?

utterances.speaker: STIPAN KRALJEVIC
utterances.text: There were various individuals either from Ilok or from elsewhere who would come, break into houses during the night, plunder, beat people, expel them, et cetera. There were many instances of that kind and this was particularly apparent from the statements, and these incidents were mostly happening in Bapska and Sarengrad because there was a lower level of presence of monitors and that is why there was a higher incidence of such cases.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: And, Mr. Kraljevic, you've said that there were various individuals who were engaged in this behaviour. When you were a mayor in exile, did you ever hear that there were any groups that were described as having engaged in this behaviour, members of any group?

utterances.speaker: STIPAN KRALJEVIC
utterances.text: Well, there were various groups in the area of Ilok dressed in military uniforms. There were many of them. There were references made to Red Berets, Seselj's men. These people were wearing various uniforms. They would sometimes identify themselves by a variety of names. They would burst into people's houses pretending to be policemen and identify themselves as policemen although they were not.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: I'd like the assistance of the Registrar, please, to pull up 65 ter 01407. This is at tab 17.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Ms. Clanton, I'm told that you are running out of time. How long would you --

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: This is my last series of questions, I think not more than five or ten minutes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: Mr. Kraljevic, do you recognise this as a document that you provided to the investigators of the Office of the Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: STIPAN KRALJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: And if you could assist, can you tell us, as it's marked as illegible in the English, what the title of this document is on the page that's in front of you?

utterances.speaker: STIPAN KRALJEVIC
utterances.text: It says the list of persons expelled between the 1st of January, 1973, but I cannot see the exact date. Anyway, it's November of the same year. And we can see below the list of the expellees, their names, their date of birth --

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: I need to ask you to pause for a moment, please.

utterances.speaker: STIPAN KRALJEVIC
utterances.text: And the place of birth.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: A moment ago, we asked -- I asked you what the title of the list was and you said that these were people that were expelled in 1973; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: STIPAN KRALJEVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, 1993.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: Thank you. And you've clarified that the date that is difficult to read is the 20th of -- did you say November, 1993?

utterances.speaker: STIPAN KRALJEVIC
utterances.text: Now I can see, it's the 20th. I can see better now.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: Thank you for assisting with that.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: If the Registrar could assist by going to the last page, please. Sorry, it's page 5, I believe.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The year is the same, only it's a continuation covering the period between the 20th of November and 31st of December, 1993.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: Thank you for providing the dates. I would like to ask you now, go back to what you were saying a moment ago about this list. I want to confirm that what you've told us is that this is a list of people -- just one moment, please. You said these were people who lived in Ilok and it has their names and their dates of birth. What other information is provided here?

utterances.speaker: STIPAN KRALJEVIC
utterances.text: And the dates of expulsion. I don't see any other details. The name of the street and when the person was expelled.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: Mr. Kraljevic, on this list, for example, the first line on the page that's currently displayed which says Marijan Solakovic, this person is listed next to the town Ilok. I'd like for you to tell us --

utterances.speaker: STIPAN KRALJEVIC
utterances.text: Bapska.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Bapska, you're right. I would like for you to tell us whether this list includes the surrounding communities of Ilok.

utterances.speaker: STIPAN KRALJEVIC
utterances.text: This list contains the names only of the people from the area where I was mayor, that is to say, Ilok, Sarengrad, Bapska, and Mohovo. So these lists pertain only to these places, Sarengrad, Bapska, Mohovo. There was approximately 10.000 inhabitants in that area.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: And Mr. Kraljevic, just to clarify your last answer, you said that the list contains the names of people who were expelled from the area that is part of Ilok, and that was Sarengrad, Bapska, and Mohovo. Does the list also include people who were expelled from the town of Ilok itself?

utterances.speaker: STIPAN KRALJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: Your Honours, I would like to have this document admitted, please, 65 ter 00417, into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It shall be assigned Exhibit Number P0226. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: Your Honour, at this time I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Mr. Kraljevic. My name is Zoran Zivanovic. I'm Defence counsel of Goran Hadzic. Let me ask you first, on page 31, you said that the situation was calm for as long as Grahovac was there, who was in charge in maintaining law and order in Ilok, and that this situation prevailed until January. Can you tell us the year?

utterances.speaker: STIPAN KRALJEVIC
utterances.text: 1992. A day or two later, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: According to your information, because I know you were not there on the spot, was this area still under the JNA control after that period?

utterances.speaker: STIPAN KRALJEVIC
utterances.text: I said that it was relatively peaceful, but even before the killing of the people in Ilok, it was relatively peaceful. I'm sorry for putting it like this. I'm sorry -- I believe that the army had no influence on the events any longer.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I have different information.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we now see a document, a document of an international organisation that was on mission in Yugoslavia, 1D404. They made a survey of human rights. I think the report has not been translated. It's a very long report and not all of it is significant, but I will read out an excerpt that refers to Ilok. It's on page 5. It's the last paragraph. I will not read out all of it because it is mostly about known facts discussed here. But the last paragraph reads: "[In English] The mission has evidence that Ilok is not under civilian administration but under direct rule of JNA and paramilitary forces."

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's why I'm asking if you are certain that the relevant time is January 1992 because if we look at this report, we will see on the cover page that it was made in May 1992. Are you sure that the JNA no longer controlled the area from January 1992?

utterances.speaker: STIPAN KRALJEVIC
utterances.text: As far as I know, Colonel Grahovac was no longer there then. If there were units of the JNA, well, I think there were such units in all of the occupied area. Now, how much influence the ones or the others had, I don't know, but most people say that the paramilitaries had more influence. But that doesn't exclude that the JNA played a part as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Let me ask you something else in connection with this. Do you know that at that time in the area there were town commands?

utterances.speaker: STIPAN KRALJEVIC
utterances.text: I personally was not involved, but I know what was generally known and I will gladly answer any question I can answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I may not have been clear enough. Do you know that after your departure from the area, did you have information to that effect that the JNA established town commands in the places that had been taken by its units?

utterances.speaker: STIPAN KRALJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, there was information that there were always some commands in place, but who took part in that command, I don't know, nor do I know the influence or how much of a say any given group had.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Now I would like us to see the following. You spoke about the negotiations process with Colonel Grahovac, later with Arandjelovic and co-workers. Here's what I would like to know: During those negotiations, did you have contact with the government in Zagreb? Did you get instructions from them concerning the demands of the JNA?

utterances.speaker: STIPAN KRALJEVIC
utterances.text: I personally didn't have such contact but some members did. For example, Ivan Uros, who left Ilok, he was a member of parliament. I think that he left on the 30th of September and went to Zagreb. As far as I know, there were contacts but I'm not sure how that went, by phone or in another way.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: When you mentioned him, you said that on the 30th of September, he went to Zagreb?

utterances.speaker: STIPAN KRALJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Actually he didn't go to Zagreb. He went to Belgrade and Skopje and then made it to Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: But I'm interested to hear if anybody of you who stayed at Ilok during those negotiations with the JNA, did any of these persons have contact with the government in Zagreb to inform them of the demands of the JNA and ask for instructions what should be done?

utterances.speaker: STIPAN KRALJEVIC
utterances.text: I don't know that. But two or three representatives of the Croatian government came to Ilok after four days and spoke to JNA representatives. That is once the convoy had left. They arrived at Ilok and had talks in the castle. The talks were about the displaced persons returning to their towns and villages. That's why they had arrived. You may not have that information, but I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know if before your departure they had been in contact with the JNA to suggest them that, in other words, suggest to the army not to remove you from there?

utterances.speaker: STIPAN KRALJEVIC
utterances.text: Well, you know, I'm saying that the representatives who were at the civil protection staff did contact Zagreb, but what they spoke about, I cannot say. But I can say briefly that the advice was: You know what the situation is and you decide whether you want to leave Ilok or not. We were mature enough to make our own decisions in the Ilok case.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Let us see a document that the OTP showed you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's P2020.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: These are the minutes taken at a polling station or from -- does it refer to all of Ilok?

utterances.speaker: STIPAN KRALJEVIC
utterances.text: This was one of the polling stations in Ilok, one of five.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Was it the most important polling station?

utterances.speaker: STIPAN KRALJEVIC
utterances.text: No, it was an average polling station or even a smaller one.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please explain the last paragraph that says that a total of 508 ballots were cast and that this represents the votes of over a thousand citizens. I understood that those who voted did not only vote for themselves but also for others.

utterances.speaker: STIPAN KRALJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, for their spouses and children. If you vote for yourself and your spouse, then you get over a thousand votes, you know. It wasn't so easy to move about and people had other things to do. The situation was extremely tense and people didn't really care so much about these -- about this vote.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: You said that on the 30th [as interpreted] of October the referendum was held and you mentioned a meeting at Sid on the 14th of October, and in that context, I believe you mentioned two European monitors?

utterances.speaker: STIPAN KRALJEVIC
utterances.text: They were monitors.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, exactly. The names are Kypr and Cunningham; right?

utterances.speaker: STIPAN KRALJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell me which meeting they attended, the one after the referendum on the 14th of October?

utterances.speaker: STIPAN KRALJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. This specifically was after the referendum when the agreement about the departure was signed.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Did they have an opportunity to see the text of the agreement?

utterances.speaker: STIPAN KRALJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. There was an interpreter. We brought her along. She was a teacher of English and translated the whole text and interpreted everything that was said at the meeting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Zivanovic, I take it your purpose was not to confuse the witness on the dates, but I see that your question was: "You said that the 30th of October the referendum was held ..." You see the difficulty? And then you ask whether it was after the referendum on the 14th of October.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: That's an error in transcript. I spoke about 13th of October.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was wrongly recorded in the transcript that the date in question was the 30th of October and it has now been corrected to the 13th.

utterances.speaker: STIPAN KRALJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I understood that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: On the occasion of that meeting, did the European monitors comment what was happening, that is, on the other hand, the proposals of the JNA, on the other hand, what you were requesting?

utterances.speaker: STIPAN KRALJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. They asked questions but did not comment. They only wanted to hear the opinions of the two sides. But not often, it was only twice or three times.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember what was being discussed?

utterances.speaker: STIPAN KRALJEVIC
utterances.text: They wanted to know why people were leaving the town because it seemed strange to them that anybody was willing to leave their homes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Whom did they ask? You? I mean, I don't mean you personally?

utterances.speaker: STIPAN KRALJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, they asked us. But they were also interested in hearing from the army why people had to leave the town.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: And what kind of answer did they get?

utterances.speaker: STIPAN KRALJEVIC
utterances.text: From me or ...

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The speakers are overlapping.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe I explained why we were leaving our homes, and the General said that they had to enter to preserve law and order. It was very -- it was a very brief explanation.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] They didn't comment that in any way?

utterances.speaker: STIPAN KRALJEVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: You said that a meeting was held on the 11th of October, 1991, also with the JNA?

utterances.speaker: STIPAN KRALJEVIC
utterances.text: With General Arandjelovic, at Sid.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: On that occasion, there was discussion about the JNA action at Lovas that had happened on the previous day, the 10th?

utterances.speaker: STIPAN KRALJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: And that meeting was attended by Rendulic, Adam Rendulic?

utterances.speaker: STIPAN KRALJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: He's from Lovas?

utterances.speaker: STIPAN KRALJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, was the manager of the co-op.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know when he came to Ilok?

utterances.speaker: STIPAN KRALJEVIC
utterances.text: I don't know when exactly but there were -- people were coming from Lovas to Ilok on a number of occasions. Whether he went to and fro, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Was he in Lovas when the JNA attacked?

utterances.speaker: STIPAN KRALJEVIC
utterances.text: I don't know. I cannot answer that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I'll immediately explain why I'm asking because I see that at that meeting, it was mentioned that 22 people were killed in Lovas?

utterances.speaker: STIPAN KRALJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: That's why I'm interested to hear how it happened that you knew on the following day how many people had been killed?

utterances.speaker: STIPAN KRALJEVIC
utterances.text: Some of the population of Lovas fled in our direction. I didn't say that they knew the exact number but that there had -- but they said that they -- there had been many victims, about 20 or so. And then a grave was also dug up. And Hugh Cunningham, the observer, also went to Lovas and spoke to Mr. Devetak, who confirmed that. He also got a list, and I saw the list of people.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I just wanted to hear whether as early as the 11th of October you had the exact number of casualties or if you just knew that there had been casualties but didn't know the exact number.

utterances.speaker: STIPAN KRALJEVIC
utterances.text: There was talk about 20-odd casualties.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: You also said that General Arandjelovic told you on that occasion that many people were killed as an act of revenge for a soldier that had been killed, but you said that no soldiers were killed in Lovas?

utterances.speaker: STIPAN KRALJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. It was never published, any kind of information was never published that a soldier had been killed. I just think that was a kind of excuse or pretext to justify the crime of this magnitude.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: In other words, since you couldn't read or hear about that anywhere else, you don't think that that actually happened, that that was just an excuse?

utterances.speaker: STIPAN KRALJEVIC
utterances.text: It was never mentioned again. Nobody ever mentioned his name or the fact that a soldier was killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: The Prosecutor showed you document P316.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If we can have it again, please. I believe that is a letter sent to Bapska.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I can see here that he says that Bapska was a peaceful place and the population was requested to submit their weapons. Were you aware of the existence of any weapons in Bapska?

utterances.speaker: STIPAN KRALJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, there were rifles but in the possession of the civilian protection.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: When you say "civilian protection," what are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: STIPAN KRALJEVIC
utterances.text: I'm referring to the residents of Bapska.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: In other words, those were not members of the Croatian Guards Corps or the MUP?

utterances.speaker: STIPAN KRALJEVIC
utterances.text: Well, there were their representatives as well, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: And they decided not to accept this but chose to withdraw to Ilok?

utterances.speaker: STIPAN KRALJEVIC
utterances.text: Well, the population was fleeing and leaving, but they refused to accept this ultimatum.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: They didn't want to surrender the weapons; is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: STIPAN KRALJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Just one clarification. You said that before all these conflicts started, certain Serbs used to spend the night in Backa Palanka.

utterances.speaker: STIPAN KRALJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: How do you know that? How do you know that they only went there to spend the night?

utterances.speaker: STIPAN KRALJEVIC
utterances.text: Well, that was common knowledge. I don't know. There were articles in newspapers about that. But these people did indeed go over there to spend the night in order to create some kind of psychological pressure. Everybody used to say that this was organised from the outside in order to portray the situation of uncertainty for people in Ilok. I believe that that was the only reason. I don't think that they were really afraid but, rather, they wanted to create an atmosphere of fear.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: But I don't understand how can you create an atmosphere of fear if these people come back and spend the whole day in Ilok. If something bad was to happen to them, it could happen during the day as well?

utterances.speaker: STIPAN KRALJEVIC
utterances.text: Well, I don't know. Everybody was playing games. Look, for example, the daily "Politika" wrote at the time that 11 people were killed in Ilok and their bodies were displayed in the square for people to see. This was a totally unprovoked fabrication. There was no conflict.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: One more thing. You said that about five Ilok policemen refused to put on the new Croatian coat of arms. Are you referring to the checkered coat of arms?

utterances.speaker: STIPAN KRALJEVIC
utterances.text: Well, you can call it that although we prefer to call it the Croatian coat of arms.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know why they refused to wear it?

utterances.speaker: STIPAN KRALJEVIC
utterances.text: They know that themselves, but there's also some kind of atmosphere being created there that this is a coat of arms associated with the Ustasha, not with Croats.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kraljevic, thank you very much. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: STIPAN KRALJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Ms. Clanton, do you have anything in redirect?

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: You don't?

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kraljevic, this is the end of your testimony. You are released as a witness. We thank you very much for coming to The Hague to assist us, and we wish you a safe journey home. The Court Usher will escort you out of court. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, too, Your Honours. It was a pleasure to testify here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Olmsted.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I have the unfortunate job of informing you that we do not have another witness this week. This is the result of a number of things. First and foremost, the waiver issue with regard to the witness -- I don't know if he has --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: He has. He has.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: -- protective measures so I don't want to mention his -- he was again scheduled this week. He couldn't come and therefore we had to scramble to find additional witnesses, and this is the best we could do at this stage. A number of witnesses that we've already scheduled or already arranged them four or five times, and we just could not get someone here to fill that potential gap. Secondly, the cross-examinations were much shorter than anticipated. Again, we've raised this before. It would be helpful if the Defence could give us at least a week or two notice of how long they intend to cross at least at the point of -- obviously they don't know what we're going to ask on direct examination, but just based upon what they believe they can, that would help us a little bit in anticipating that there would be these kind of gaps. But we -- I think next week we have a full schedule, so hopefully it's going to work out fine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Okay. In the meantime, I hope that instead of court time, you will enjoy the sunshine.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Your Honour, we will.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: If that's all, court adjourned. ---Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 1.59 p.m., to be reconvened on Monday, the 10th day of June, 2013
